cards.title: Two Pointers: Overview
cards.heading: Turn O(n²) into O(n)
cards.body:
**Two Pointers** starts at opposite ends of a **sorted array** and moves toward the center.

Instead of checking all pairs with nested loops, each pointer move eliminates multiple impossible pairs — leveraging the sorted property to skip work.

If sum is too large? Move `right` left. Too small? Move `left` right.
cards.summary: Use two pointers starting at opposite ends of a sorted array to find pairs that meet criteria in O(n) time.

cards.title: Container With Most Water
cards.heading: Two walls, max water area
cards.body:
Pick any two vertical lines from an array to form a container. The **area** is width × height:
- **Width**: distance between the two lines
- **Height**: the shorter wall (water overflows there)

Goal: find the max area in O(n) time.
cards.summary: Pick two vertical lines from an array to form a container. Return the maximum water area (width × shorter wall).

cards.title: Container With Most Water
cards.heading: Always move the shorter wall
cards.body:
Start pointers at both ends (widest container). Why move the shorter wall?

**Moving the taller wall can never help** because:
- Width decreases
- Height is still capped by the shorter wall

So we move the shorter wall, hoping to find a taller one.

cards.title: Two Sum (Sorted Array)
cards.heading: Two pointers eliminate impossible pairs
cards.body:
In a **sorted** array, start pointers at both ends.

- Sum too **small**? Move left → (bigger number)
- Sum too **large**? Move right ← (smaller number)

Each move eliminates an entire class of pairs. **O(n) time, O(1) space.**
cards.summary: Find if a pair of numbers in a sorted array sums to a target using two pointers to eliminate unnecessary pairs.

cards.title: Two Sum (Sorted Array)
cards.heading: Why sortedness matters
cards.body:
Moving a pointer changes the sum **predictably**:
- Left pointer → always increases sum
- Right pointer ← always decreases sum

Without sorting, you can't decide which pointer to move.

cards.title: 3-Sum
cards.heading: 3-Sum = Sort + Two Pointers
cards.body:
Fix one number `nums[i]`, then find **two numbers** in the rest that sum to `-nums[i]`.

- **Sort first** so you can use two pointers
- **Skip duplicates** at both the outer loop and inner pointers to ensure unique triplets
- Time: **O(n²)** — outer loop × inner two-pointer scan
cards.summary: Find all unique triplets in an array that sum to zero using sorting and two pointers.

cards.title: 3-Sum
cards.heading: The Duplicate-Skipping Dance
cards.body:
**Outer loop:** `if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i-1]: continue`

**After finding a triplet:**
- Skip `left` forward while `nums[left] == nums[left+1]`
- Skip `right` backward while `nums[right] == nums[right-1]`
- Then move both pointers one more step

Without this, you'll get duplicate triplets.

cards.title: Valid Triangle Number
cards.heading: Sort first, check once
cards.body:
For sorted sides **a ≤ b ≤ c**, valid triangles only need `a + b > c`.

The other two inequalities are **automatic**:
- `a + c > b` holds since `c ≥ b`
- `b + c > a` holds since `b ≥ a`

Sort the array, fix the largest side, and use **two pointers** to count valid pairs.
cards.summary: Count triplets in an array that can form valid triangle sides using the triangle inequality after sorting.

cards.title: Valid Triangle Number
cards.heading: Count in batches, not one-by-one
cards.body:
When `nums[left] + nums[right] > nums[i]`, **every** index from `left` to `right - 1` also forms a valid triplet with `right` and `i`.

Add `right - left` to the count in **one step**, then shrink the window by decrementing `right`.
cards.summary: Count triplets in an array that can form valid triangle sides using the triangle inequality after sorting.

cards.title: Valid Triangle Number
cards.label: Solution · Python
cards.code:
def triangleNumber(nums):
    """
    Count triplets that can form valid triangle sides.
    
    Uses triangle inequality: for sorted a ≤ b ≤ c, only check a + b > c.
    """
    nums.sort()
    count = 0
    
    for i in range(len(nums) - 1, 1, -1):
        left = 0
        right = i - 1
        
        while left < right:
            if nums[left] + nums[right] > nums[i]:
                count += right - left
                right -= 1
            else:
                left += 1
    
    return count
cards.summary: Count triplets in an array that can form valid triangle sides using the triangle inequality after sorting.

options: Because the other two conditions are always false for sorted values
Because the other two conditions are automatically satisfied when c ≥ b ≥ a
Because sorting guarantees that all triplets form valid triangles
Because we only care about the largest side when checking triangle validity
cards.explain: When a ≤ b ≤ c, if a + b > c holds, then a + c > b and b + c > a are automatically true.
cards.summary: Count triplets in an array that can form valid triangle sides using the triangle inequality after sorting.

cards.heading: Two pointers, one job
cards.body: One pointer scans the array, the other tracks where to **place** the next non-zero. Swap when you find a non-zero, increment the placement pointer. Zeros naturally slide to the end — no extra pass needed.

cards.title: Sort Colors
cards.heading: Three pointers, one pass
cards.body:
The **Dutch National Flag** algorithm sorts 0s, 1s, and 2s in one pass using three pointers:

- **left**: boundary of 0s
- **i**: current element
- **right**: boundary of 2s

Partition in-place by moving 0s to `left`, 2s to `right`, leaving 1s in the middle.

cards.title: Sort Colors
cards.heading: Why we don't move i
cards.body:
**Critical gotcha:** When `nums[i] == 2`, we swap with `nums[right]` and decrement `right`, but **don't increment i**.

Why? The new value at `i` came from the unsorted region — it could be 0, 1, or 2. We must examine it next iteration.

cards.title: Fixed-Length Sliding Window
cards.heading: Slide, Don't Recompute
cards.body:
A **fixed-length sliding window** keeps exactly **k** elements. Each step: **add** the new element, **remove** the old one — in O(1).

- Use when the subarray/substring length is **known**.
- Avoids recalculating from scratch every position.
- Turns O(nk) brute force into O(n).
cards.summary: Slide a window of fixed size k through an array, updating state incrementally in O(1) per element.

cards.title: Fixed-Length Sliding Window
cards.heading: Recognize the Pattern
cards.body:
Use fixed-length sliding window when:

- Problem asks for a **contiguous** subarray or substring
- The **length k is given**
- You need max/min/count over all size-k subarrays

**Example**: "Find max sum of any subarray of size k."

options: When the input array is sorted in ascending order
When you know the exact length of the subarray or substring you're looking for
When the elements you need aren't contiguous in the input
When the window's validity depends on satisfying a constraint rather than reaching a known size
cards.explain: Fixed-length is for when the problem specifies exact size k; variable-length is for constraint-based sizing.

cards.title: Maximum Sum of Subarrays of Size K
cards.heading: Slide the window, not the sum
cards.body:
**Fixed-size sliding window** finds max subarray sum in O(n).

Instead of recalculating the entire sum for each k-element window:
- **Add** the new element entering
- **Subtract** the old element leaving

One pass. Constant work per window.
cards.summary: Find the maximum sum among all contiguous subarrays of size k using a fixed-size sliding window with incremental sum updates.

cards.title: Maximum Sum of Subarrays of Size K
cards.heading: When to slide the window
cards.body:
Expand the window until it reaches size `k`.

Once `end - start + 1 == k`:
1. Update max_sum
2. **Slide**: subtract `nums[start]`, increment `start`

Repeat until the end pointer has visited every element.
cards.summary: Find the maximum sum among all contiguous subarrays of size k using a fixed-size sliding window with incremental sum updates.

cards.title: Maximum Sum of Subarrays of Size K
cards.label: Crux · Python
cards.code:
def max_subarray_sum(nums, k):
    max_sum = float('-inf')
    current_sum = 0
    start = 0
    
    for end in range(len(nums)):
        current_sum += nums[end]
        
        if end - start + 1 == k:
            max_sum = max(max_sum, current_sum)
            current_sum -= nums[start]
            start += 1
    
    return max_sum
cards.summary: Find the maximum sum among all contiguous subarrays of size k using a fixed-size sliding window with incremental sum updates.

cards.title: Maximum Sum of Subarrays of Size K
cards.q: Why is the sliding window approach O(n) instead of O(n*k)?
options: It uses a hash map to cache previous sums
It updates the sum incrementally by adding one element and removing one element per window
It processes only k elements total instead of n elements
It uses binary search to find the maximum sum
cards.explain: Constant work per window (add one, subtract one) avoids recalculating the entire k-element sum each time.
cards.summary: Find the maximum sum among all contiguous subarrays of size k using a fixed-size sliding window with incremental sum updates.

cards.title: Max Points You Can Obtain From Cards
cards.heading: Pick from ends, think from middle
cards.body:
Picking **k cards from either end** leaves **(n - k) consecutive cards** in the middle.

**The insight:** `sum_picked = total - sum_unpicked`

To **maximize** what you pick, **minimize** what you leave behind. Find the minimum-sum window of size **(n - k)**.
cards.summary: Maximize score by picking k cards from array ends by finding minimum sum window of size n-k in middle

cards.title: Max Points You Can Obtain From Cards
cards.heading: One window, all possibilities
cards.body:
Every way to pick k cards from the ends = one window of (n - k) cards you skip.

- First 3 cards → skip window at end
- Last 3 cards → skip window at start
- First 1 + last 2 → skip window in middle

Slide the window once, track the **min sum**, done.
cards.summary: Maximize score by picking k cards from array ends by finding minimum sum window of size n-k in middle

cards.title: Max Points You Can Obtain From Cards
cards.label: Solution · Python
cards.code:
def maxScore(cards, k):
    """Find max score by picking k cards from either end."""
    total = sum(cards)
    if k == len(cards):
        return total
    
    window_sum = 0
    max_points = 0
    start = 0
    
    for end in range(len(cards)):
        window_sum += cards[end]
        
        if end - start + 1 == len(cards) - k:
            max_points = max(total - window_sum, max_points)
            window_sum -= cards[start]
            start += 1
    
    return max_points
cards.summary: Maximize score by picking k cards from array ends by finding minimum sum window of size n-k in middle

cards.title: Max Points You Can Obtain From Cards
cards.q: Why do we find the minimum sum window of size n-k instead of directly trying all combinations of picking from the ends?
options: Because picking k cards from ends leaves n-k cards in middle, and maximizing picked cards means minimizing unpicked cards
Because the minimum window is always at the beginning of the array
Because we need to avoid using extra space for tracking all combinations
Because the sliding window technique is faster than any other approach
cards.explain: sum of picked = total - sum of unpicked. To maximize picked, minimize unpicked.
cards.summary: Maximize score by picking k cards from array ends by finding minimum sum window of size n-k in middle

cards.title: Max Sum of Distinct Subarrays of Length K
cards.heading: Fixed Window + Distinct Check
cards.body:
Track a **sliding window of size k** with a hash map. The window is valid only when `len(state) == k` — meaning all k elements are distinct.

- Use `curr_sum` to track running total
- Add element → expand; remove element → contract
- Check distinctness before updating max
cards.summary: Find the maximum sum of a subarray of length k where all elements are distinct, or return 0 if no such subarray exists.

cards.title: Max Sum of Distinct Subarrays of Length K
cards.heading: Why len(state) == k?
cards.body:
If your window has **k elements** and your hash map has **k keys**, each element appears exactly once.

Duplicates collapse to one key → fewer keys → `len(state) < k` → skip this window.
cards.summary: Find the maximum sum of a subarray of length k where all elements are distinct, or return 0 if no such subarray exists.

cards.title: Max Sum of Distinct Subarrays of Length K
cards.label: Core Logic · Python
cards.code:
for end in range(len(nums)):
    curr_sum += nums[end]
    state[nums[end]] = state.get(nums[end], 0) + 1
    
    if end - start + 1 == k:
        if len(state) == k:  # all distinct
            max_sum = max(max_sum, curr_sum)
        # Contract window
        curr_sum -= nums[start]
        state[nums[start]] -= 1
        if state[nums[start]] == 0:
            del state[nums[start]]  # keep map clean
        start += 1

cards.title: Max Sum of Distinct Subarrays of Length K
cards.q: Why do we compare len(state) == k to determine if all elements are distinct?
options: Because len(state) counts the total number of elements in the window
Because if k elements are in the window and state has k keys, each element appears exactly once
Because state automatically removes duplicates from the array
Because len(state) returns the sum of all frequencies in the dictionary
cards.explain: If the window has k elements and state has k keys, each element is unique (no duplicates share a key).
cards.summary: Find the maximum sum of a subarray of length k where all elements are distinct, or return 0 if no such subarray exists.

cards.title: Variable-Length Sliding Window
cards.heading: Two pointers that move independently
cards.body:
**Variable-length sliding window** expands (`end++`) and contracts (`start++`) to find the longest/shortest subarray satisfying a condition.

Unlike fixed windows, the size isn't known — you discover it by greedily expanding and only contracting when the constraint breaks.

**O(n) time** because each element is visited at most twice.
cards.summary: Expand and contract a window to find the longest/shortest subarray satisfying a condition in O(n) time.

cards.title: Variable-Length Sliding Window
cards.heading: When to use it
cards.body:
Recognize it when you see:
- **Longest** or **shortest** contiguous subarray/substring
- Constraints like "at most k distinct", "without repeating", "sum ≥ target"
- Brute force O(n²) would be too slow

Examples: longest substring without repeating characters, smallest subarray with sum ≥ S.
cards.summary: Expand and contract a window to find the longest/shortest subarray satisfying a condition in O(n) time.

cards.label: Crux · Python

start = 0
state = {}  # track window contents
max_length = 0

for end in range(len(nums)):
    state[nums[end]] = state.get(nums[end], 0) + 1
    
    # Contract while invalid
    while is_invalid(state):
        state[nums[start]] -= 1

Fixed-length has a known window size, variable-length discovers the optimal size dynamically
Fixed-length runs in O(n²), variable-length runs in O(n)
Fixed-length uses arrays, variable-length uses hash maps

cards.heading: Jump past duplicates instantly
cards.body:
Track the **last index** of each character in a dict. When you hit a duplicate, move your left pointer **past the previous occurrence** in one hop—no need to shrink incrementally.

**Trick:** `start = max(start, state[char] + 1)` ensures the window never moves backward.

cards.heading: When to use variable window
cards.body:
Use a **variable-length sliding window** when you need to find the longest (or shortest) valid substring and the window size isn't fixed.

**Pattern:** expand right, then contract left **only when** you violate a constraint (here: duplicate characters).

cards.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
cards.heading: Valid window = k replacements
cards.body:
A window is **valid** when:
`window_length - max_freq <= k`

**Why?** `window_length - max_freq` = replacements needed. If the most frequent character appears 3× in a window of 5, you need **2 replacements** to make all chars identical.

Goal: find the longest valid window.

cards.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
cards.heading: Don't update max_freq downward
cards.body:
`max_freq` tracks the **historical maximum** frequency, not just the current window.

**Why leave it?** We only care about windows *longer* than what we've found. This lets us skip unnecessary shrinks and keeps the algorithm O(n).

cards.title: Intervals: Overview
cards.heading: Sort, then sweep
cards.body:
Intervals = `[start, end]` pairs (meetings, time slots). The trick: **sort by start time**, then sweep through.

After sorting, you only compare each interval with the **previous one** — no nested loops needed.

Sorting transforms chaos into structure.

def canAttendMeetings(intervals):
    """
    Determine if a person can attend all meetings without conflicts.
    
    Args:
        intervals: List of meeting intervals [start, end]
    
    Returns:
        bool: True if no overlapping meetings, False otherwise
    """
    if not intervals:
        return True
    
    intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    
    for i in range(1, len(intervals)):
        if intervals[i][0] < intervals[i-1][1]:
            return False
    
    return True

**Phase 3:** Append the rest

cards.title: Non-Overlapping Intervals
cards.label: Solution · Python
cards.code:
def nonOverlappingIntervals(intervals):
    """
    Return minimum number of intervals to remove for non-overlapping remainder.
    
    Args:
        intervals: List of [start, end] interval pairs
        
    Returns:
        Minimum number of intervals to remove
        
    Example:
        >>> nonOverlappingIntervals([[1,3],[5,8],[4,10],[11,13]])
        1
    """
    if not intervals:
        return 0
    
    # Sort by end time for greedy selection
    intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[1])
    
    # Track end of last kept interval and count of kept intervals
    end = intervals[0][1]
    count = 1
    
    for i in range(1, len(intervals)):
        # Non-overlapping interval found
        if intervals[i][0] >= end:
            end = intervals[i][1]
            count += 1
    
    # Return number of intervals to remove
    return len(intervals) - count
cards.summary: Find the minimum number of intervals to remove so remaining intervals don't overlap using greedy end-time sorting.

cards.label: Solution · Python
cards.code:
def decodeString(s):
    """Decode an encoded string where k[encoded_string] means repeat k times.
    
    Args:
        s: Encoded string with pattern k[encoded_string]
        
    Returns:
        Decoded string with all patterns expanded
        
    Example:
        >>> decodeString("3[a2[c]]")
        'accaccacc'
        >>> decodeString("2[abc]3[cd]ef")
        'abcabccdcdcdef'
    """
    stack = []
    curr_string = ""
    current_number = 0
    
    for char in s:
        if char == "[":
            stack.append(curr_string)
            stack.append(current_number)
            curr_string = ""
            current_number = 0
        elif char == "]":
            num = stack.pop()
            prev_string = stack.pop()
            curr_string = prev_string + num * curr_string
        elif char.isdigit():
            current_number = current_number * 10 + int(char)
        else:
            curr_string += char
    
    return curr_string
cards.summary: Decode an encoded string where k[encoded_string] means repeat the string k times. Brackets can be nested.

cards.heading: Nodes strung together, no array
cards.body:
A **linked list** is nodes in sequence—each has a `val` and `next` pointer. The first node is the **head**, the last is **tail** (`next=None`).

```python
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next
```

cards.heading: Fast/slow pointers find the middle
cards.body:
Two pointers from `head`: `slow` steps once, `fast` steps twice per loop.

When `fast` hits the end, `slow` is at the **middle**.

**Gotcha**: For even-length lists, you get the *second* middle node.

Also detects **cycles**: if `fast == slow` mid-loop, there's a cycle.

def reverse(head):
    prev = None
    current = head
    while current:
        next_ = current.next
        current.next = prev  # flip pointer
        prev = current
        current = next_
    return prev

def is_palindrome(head):
    """Check if a singly linked list is a palindrome.
    
    Args:
        head: The head node of the linked list
        
    Returns:
        bool: True if the list is a palindrome, False otherwise
    """
    # Find middle of the linked list using fast and slow pointers
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        fast = fast.next.next
        slow = slow.next
    
    # Reverse second half of the list
    curr, prev = slow, None
    while curr:
        next_ = curr.next  # Save next node
        curr.next = prev   # Reverse pointer
        prev = curr        # Move pointers
        curr = next_
    
    # Check palindrome by comparing halves
    left, right = head, prev
    while right:
        if left.val != right.val:
            return False
        left = left.next
        right = right.next
    
    return True

Without a dummy, removing the head is a special case (no predecessor).

cards.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
cards.label: Solution · Python
cards.code:
def removeNthFromEnd(head, n):
    """
    Remove the nth node from the end of a singly linked list.
    
    Args:
        head: ListNode - head of the singly linked list
        n: int - position from the end (1-indexed)
    
    Returns:
        ListNode - head of the modified list
    """
    # Create dummy node to handle edge case of removing head
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    dummy.next = head
    fast = dummy
    slow = dummy
    
    # Move fast pointer n steps ahead to create n-node gap
    for i in range(n):
        fast = fast.next
    
    # Move both pointers until fast reaches end
    # When fast is at last node, slow will be at node before target
    while fast.next is not None:
        fast = fast.next
        slow = slow.next
    
    # Remove the nth node from end by skipping it
    slow.next = slow.next.next
    
    return dummy.next

    dummy.next = head
    prev = dummy

        first = prev.next
        second = first.next
        
        prev.next = second
        first.next = second.next
        second.next = first
        
        prev = first
    
    return dummy.next

The answer lies between **max(nums)** and **sum(nums)**. Instead of searching for an element, we **binary search the space of possible answers**.

- Start a new subarray when adding the next element would exceed the max
- Return true if total subarrays ≤ k

cards.title: Split Array Largest Sum

cards.code:
def splitArray(nums, k):
    """
    Split array into k contiguous subarrays minimizing the maximum subarray sum.
    Uses binary search on the answer space with greedy feasibility check.
    
    Time: O(n * log(sum)) where sum is the total of all elements
    Space: O(1)
    """
    def canSplit(maxSum):
        """Check if we can split into <= k subarrays with max sum <= maxSum."""
        subarrays = 1
        currentSum = 0
        
        for num in nums:
            if currentSum + num > maxSum:
                # Start new subarray
                subarrays += 1
                currentSum = num
            else:
                currentSum += num
        
        return subarrays <= k
    
    # Binary search bounds
    left = max(nums)  # Minimum possible: largest element
    right = sum(nums)  # Maximum possible: all in one subarray
    
    # Binary search for minimum valid max-sum
    while left < right:
        mid = (left + right) // 2
        if canSplit(mid):
            # Can split with this max, try smaller
            right = mid
        else:
            # Cannot split, need larger max
            left = mid + 1
    
    return left
cards.summary: Split array into k contiguous subarrays to minimize the maximum subarray sum using binary search on the answer space.

**Monotonic property**: if capacity `c` works (≤ maxBoxes), then any larger capacity also works—bigger boxes mean fewer boxes.

cards.title: Minimum Shipping Capacity
cards.label: Solution · Python
cards.code:
def minimumShippingCapacity(quantities, weights, maxBoxes, maxWeightPerBox):
    """
    Find minimum box capacity to ship all products within box limit.
    
    Args:
        quantities: List of item counts per product
        weights: List of weight per item (kg) for each product
        maxBoxes: Maximum number of boxes allowed
        maxWeightPerBox: Maximum weight per box (kg)
    
    Returns:
        Minimum capacity (items per box) needed
    """
    def countBoxes(capacity):
        boxes = 0
        for i in range(len(quantities)):
            remaining = quantities[i]
            while remaining > 0:
                # Items this box = min(capacity limit, weight limit, items left)
                itemsThisBox = min(
                    capacity,
                    maxWeightPerBox // weights[i],
                    remaining
                )
                boxes += 1
                remaining -= itemsThisBox
        return boxes
    
    # Binary search on capacity
    left = 1
    right = max(quantities)
    
    while left < right:
        mid = (left + right) // 2
        if countBoxes(mid) <= maxBoxes:
            right = mid  # Capacity works, try smaller
        else:
            left = mid + 1  # Capacity too small, search larger
    
    return left

cards.title: Merge K Sorted Lists
cards.label: Solution · Python
cards.code:
from heapq import heappush, heappop

def mergeKLists(lists):
    """
    Merge k sorted linked lists into one sorted linked list.
    
    Args:
        lists: List of k sorted linked list heads
    
    Returns:
        Head of the merged sorted linked list
    """
    if not lists:
        return None
    
    # Filter out empty lists
    non_empty = [head for head in lists if head]
    if not non_empty:
        return None
    
    # Initialize heap with head of each list
    # Use (val, id, node) to avoid comparing nodes
    heap = []
    for head in non_empty:
        heappush(heap, (head.val, id(head), head))
    
    # Build merged list using dummy head
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    current = dummy
    
    # Extract minimum and add its successor
    while heap:
        val, _, node = heappop(heap)
        current.next = node
        current = current.next
        
        if node.next:
            heappush(heap, (node.next.val, id(node.next), node.next))
    
    return dummy.next

cards.heading: What is Tree Tilt?

A node's **tilt** = |left subtree sum - right subtree sum|

- Leaf nodes have tilt 0 (both subtrees empty)
- Missing children count as sum 0

cards.label: Crux · Python

def findTilt(root):
    tilt = 0
    
    def dfs(node):
        nonlocal tilt
        if not node:
            return 0
        
        left = dfs(node.left)
        right = dfs(node.right)
        
        tilt += abs(left - right)
        return left + right + node.val
    
    dfs(root)
    return tilt

def diameterOfBinaryTree(root):
    max_diameter = 0
    
    def dfs(node):
        nonlocal max_diameter
        if not node:
            return 0
        
        left = dfs(node.left)
        right = dfs(node.right)
        
        # update global max
        max_diameter = max(max_diameter, left + right)
        
        # return height to parent
        return 1 + max(left, right)
    
    dfs(root)
    return max_diameter

- No cycles

cards.body:

**Without parent tracking:** you'd flag the edge A↔B as a cycle.

**Key:** A cycle exists only if you hit a visited node that's NOT your parent.

cards.title: Matrices (Grid DFS)
cards.heading: Grids are graphs in disguise
cards.body:
Each cell is a **node**. Its neighbors? The cells **up, down, left, right**.

`grid[1][1]` has 4 neighbors:
- `grid[0][1]` (up)
- `grid[2][1]` (down)
- `grid[1][0]` (left)
- `grid[1][2]` (right)

DFS on a matrix = DFS on a graph where edges connect adjacent cells.
